title: Variables and controls
lede: How to run a fair test, and why correlation isn't causation.

sections.md:
## Three kinds of variable
| Variable | What it is | Example (testing tire pressure vs fuel economy) |
|---|---|---|
| Independent | What **you** change | Tire pressure |
| Dependent | What you **measure** | Miles per gallon |
| Controlled | What you keep the **same** | Truck, load weight, route, speed, driver |

Change one thing at a time. If you change the pressure **and** the route, you can't tell which one moved the mpg.

## Control groups
A **control group** gets no treatment, so you have something to compare against. To test a new fuel additive, run some trucks with it and some without, on the same routes.

In medicine, the control group often gets a **placebo**: a fake treatment that looks real. In a **double-blind** study, neither the patients nor the researchers know who got what, so expectations can't bend the results.

## Sample size
One trip proves nothing. Traffic, weather and luck add noise. More trials and bigger samples make results more trustworthy, because random noise averages out.

## Correlation is not causation
Two things can rise together without one causing the other. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. That hidden driver is called a **confounding variable**.

The only reliable way to show cause is an experiment where you change one thing and control the rest.

sections.title: Spot the flaw
sections.problem: A shop says: "Customers who bought our premium oil had 30% fewer breakdowns."
steps: Who buys premium oil? Probably owners who maintain trucks carefully in general.
Careful maintenance could be the real cause.
There's no control group of careful owners using regular oil.
sections.answer: **Correlation, not proven causation.** A confounding variable (careful owners) could explain it.

practice.q: You test whether music affects typing speed. The independent variable is…
In the same test, the dependent variable is…

options: To have a baseline to compare against
practice.why: Without it, you can't tell if the treatment did anything.

practice.q: Cities with more firefighters have more fire damage. Most likely explanation?
options: Bigger cities have more fires and more firefighters
practice.why: City size is the confounding variable.

options: Only patients don't know who got the real treatment
practice.why: It keeps expectations from skewing results.

practice.q: Which is the most trustworthy test of a new tire?
options: 20 trucks with new tires and 20 with old, same routes, 3 months
practice.why: Big sample, control group, same conditions.
